entries.d80bf1ee1959f0f8cc81275301ad6e1dc5f7b3e4: <div eID="gen23884" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen23885" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen23886" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen23886" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen23885" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen23887" type="x-p"/> Exhortations against becoming surety for others, <reference osisRef="Pro.6.1-Pro.6.5">Pro 6:1-5</reference>; against idleness, from the example of the ant, <reference osisRef="Pro.6.6-Pro.6.11">Pro 6:6-11</reference>; description of a worthless person, <reference osisRef="Pro.6.12-Pro.6.15">Pro 6:12-15</reference>; seven things hateful to God, <reference osisRef="Pro.6.16-Pro.6.19">Pro 6:16-19</reference>; the benefits of instruction, <reference osisRef="Pro.6.20-Pro.6.23">Pro 6:20-23</reference>; farther exhortations against bad women, and especially against adultery, <reference osisRef="Pro.6.24-Pro.6.33">Pro 6:24-33</reference>; what may be expected from jealousy, <reference osisRef="Pro.6.34">Pro 6:34</reference>, <reference osisRef="Pro.6.35">Pro 6:35</reference>. <div eID="gen23887" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23888" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen23888" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23889" type="x-p"/> If thou be surety for thy friend - לרעך lereacha, for thy neighbor; i.e., any person. If thou pledge thyself in behalf of another, thou takest the burden off him, and placest it on thine own shoulders; and when he knows he has got one to stand between him and the demands of law and justice, he will feel little responsibility; his spirit of exertion will become crippled, and listlessness as to the event will be the consequence. His own character will suffer little; his property nothing, for his friend bears all the burden: and perhaps the very person for whom he bore this burden treats him with neglect; and, lest the restoration of the pledge should be required, will avoid both the sight and presence of his friend. Give what thou canst; but, except in extreme cases, be surety for no man. Striking or shaking hands when the mouth had once made the promise, was considered as the ratification of the engagement; and thus the man became ensnared with the words of his mouth.
entries.9b6f96ca71fcdd8e1898451a350a33e47c40f9c4: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen23889" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23890" type="x-p"/> Do this - deliver thyself - Continue to press him for whom thou art become surety, to pay his creditor; give him no rest till he do it, else thou mayest fully expect to be left to pay the debt.
entries.8fab0ad09e336b40fe0928562772a76b8ac9ade8: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen23890" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23891" type="x-p"/> Deliver thyself as a roe - צבי tsebi, the antelope. If thou art got into the snare, get out if thou possibly canst; make every struggle and excertion, as the antelope taken in the net, and the bird taken in the snare would, in order to get free from thy captivity.
entries.94f0d40d8df6f05bc0acfb25777d2b46c92886a9: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen23891" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23892" type="x-p"/> Go to the ant, thou sluggard - נמלה nemalah, the ant, is a remarkable creature for foresight, industry, and economy. At the proper seasons they collect their food - not in the summer to lay up for the winter; for they sleep during the winter, and eat not; and therefore such hoards would be to them useless; but when the food necessary for them is most plentiful, then they collect it for their consumption in the proper seasons. No insect is more laborious, not even the bee itself; and none is more fondly attached to or more careful of its young, than the ant. When the young are in their aurelia state, in which they appear like a small grain of rice, they will bring them out of their nests, and lay them near their holes, for the benefit of the sun; and on the approach of rain, carefully remove them, and deposit them in the nest, the hole or entrance to which they will cover with a piece of thin stone or tile, to prevent the wet from getting in. It is a fact that they do not lay up any meat for winter; nor does Solomon, either here or in <reference osisRef="Pro.30.25">Pro 30:25</reference>, assert it. He simply says that they provide their food in summer, and gather it in harvest; these are the most proper times for a stock to be laid in for their consumption; not in winter; for no such thing appears in any of their nests, nor do they need it, as they sleep during that season; but for autumn, during which they wake and work. Spring, summer, and autumn, they are incessant in their labor; and their conduct affords a bright example to men.
entries.c91c6ee006a72b3dc8cb0be53dc6f8dbe4be6e0b: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen23892" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23893" type="x-p"/> Yet a little sleep, a little slumber - This, if not the language, is the feeling of the sluggard. The ant gathers its food in summer and in harvest, and sleeps in winter when it has no work to do. If the sluggard would work in the day, and sleep at night, it would be all proper. The ant yields him a lesson of reproach.
entries.bf95af7a2abae4980033babfac022cd40126207f: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen23893" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23894" type="x-p"/> So shall thy poverty come as one that travelleth - That is, with slow, but surely approaching steps. <div eID="gen23894" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23895" type="x-p"/> Thy want as an armed man - That is, with irresistible fury; and thou art not prepared to oppose it. The Vulgate, Septuagint, and Arabic add the following clause to this verse: - "But if thou wilt be diligent, thy harvest shall be as a fountain; and poverty shall flee far away from thee." <div eID="gen23895" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23896" type="x-p"/> It is also thus in the Old MS. Bible: If forsothe unslow thou shul ben; shul comen as a welle thi rip; and nede fer shal fleen fro thee.
entries.76e6c12b6a50208b8a8cb2aba0ee4d8b0150e7f4: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen23896" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23897" type="x-p"/> A naughty person - אדם בליעל adam beliyal, "Adam good for nothing." When he lost his innocence. A man apostata; Old MS. Bible. <div eID="gen23897" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23898" type="x-p"/> A wicked man - איש און ish aven. He soon became a general transgressor after having departed from his God. All his posterity, unless restored by Divine grace, are men of Belial, and sinners by trade; and most of them, in one form or other, answer the character here given. They yield their members instruments of unrighteousness unto sin.
entries.c325680687c6cd8334577fb2ffa7c0f7ccafc86d: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen23898" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23899" type="x-p"/> He winketh with his eyes, he speaketh with his feet, he teacheth with his fingers - These things seem to be spoken of debauchees, and the following quotation from Ovid, Amor. Iib. i., El. iv., ver. 15, shoots the whole process of the villany spoken of by Solomon: <div eID="gen23899" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23900" type="x-p"/> Cum premit ille torum, vultu comes ipsa modestoIbis, ut accumbas: clam mihi tange pedem. <div eID="gen23900" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23901" type="x-p"/> Me specta, nutusque meos, vultum que loquacemExcipe furtivas, et refer ipsa, notas. <div eID="gen23901" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23902" type="x-p"/> Verba superciliis sine voce loquentia dicamVerba leges digitis, verba notata mero. <div eID="gen23902" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23903" type="x-p"/> Cum tibi succurrit Veneris lascivia nostrae,Purpureas tenero pollice tange genas, etc., etc. <div eID="gen23903" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23904" type="x-p"/> The whole elegy is in the same strain: it is translated in Garth's Ovid, but cannot be introduced here.
entries.ac3459cf14208f230301e30a1b4109c8793093c8: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen23904" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23905" type="x-p"/> He deviseth mischief - He plots schemes and plans to bring it to pass. <div eID="gen23905" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23906" type="x-p"/> He soweth discord - Between men and their wives, by seducing the latter from their fidelity. See the preceding quotation.
entries.45c6335030ebb2b510d84f28375ee959c319321e: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen23906" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23907" type="x-p"/> Suddenly shall he be broken - Probably alluding to some punishment of the adulterer, such as being stoned to death. A multitude shall join together, and so overwhelm him with stones, that he shall have his flesh and bones broken to pieces, and there shall be no remedy - none to deliver or pity him.
entries.83e421a9f35748e6d02da108e1b02a4ba120854c: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen23907" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23908" type="x-p"/> These six - doth the Lord hate - <div eID="gen23908" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23909" type="x-p"/> 1. A proud look - exalted eyes; those who will not condescend to look on the rest of mankind. <div eID="gen23909" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23910" type="x-p"/> 2. A lying tongue - he who neither loves nor tells truth. <div eID="gen23910" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23911" type="x-p"/> 3. Hands that shed innocent blood, whether by murder or by battery. <div eID="gen23911" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23912" type="x-p"/> 4. A heart that deviseth wicked imaginations - the heart that fabricates such, lays the foundation, builds upon it, and completes the superstructure of iniquity. <div eID="gen23912" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23913" type="x-p"/> 5. Feet that be swift in running to mischief - he who works iniquity with greediness. <div eID="gen23913" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23914" type="x-p"/> 6. A false witness that speaketh lies - one who, even on his oath before a court of justice, tells any thing but the truth. <div eID="gen23914" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23915" type="x-p"/> Seven are an abomination unto him - נפשו naphsho, "to his soul." The seventh is, he that soweth discord among brethren - he who troubles the peace of a family, of a village, of the state; all who, by lies and misrepresentations, strive to make men's minds evil-affected towards their brethren.
entries.5a761a6e93dc384f756825c0b8e82abe2f6eb747: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen23915" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23916" type="x-p"/> Keep thy father's commandment - See on <reference osisRef="Pro.1.8">Pro 1:8</reference> (note).
entries.045f56e524248f42ff6ab480862db2b2dae9d576: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen23916" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23917" type="x-p"/> Bind them continually upon thine heart - See on <reference osisRef="Pro.3.3">Pro 3:3</reference> (note). And see a similar command, to which this is an allusion, <reference osisRef="Deu.6.6-Deu.6.8">Deu 6:6-8</reference> (note).
entries.eb5cd78613d420a9527df8954c964809d735b000: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen23917" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23918" type="x-p"/> When thou goest, it shall lead thee - Here the law is personified; and is represented as a nurse, teacher, and guardian, by night and day. An upright man never goes but as directed by God's word and led by God's Spirit. <div eID="gen23918" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23919" type="x-p"/> When thou sleepest - He commends his body and soul to the protection of his Maker when he lies down and sleeps in peace. And when he awakes in the morning, the promises and mercies of God are the first things that present themselves to his recollection.
entries.cdc1af98cbc66511b392525631e29c9b6f9a6e54: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen23919" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23920" type="x-p"/> For the commandment is a lamp - It illuminates our path. It shows us how we should walk and praise God. <div eID="gen23920" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23921" type="x-p"/> And the law is light - A general light, showing the nature and will of God, and the interest and duty of Man. <div eID="gen23921" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23922" type="x-p"/> And reproofs of instruction - Or, that instruction which reproves us for our sins and errors leads us into the way of life.
entries.402e4fd654246f2c01cb41fe38ed0c27e4d1c431: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen23922" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23923" type="x-p"/> To keep thee from the evil woman - Solomon had suffered sorely from this quarter; and hence his repeated cautions and warnings to others. The strange woman always means one that is not a man's own; and sometimes it may also imply a foreign harlot, one who is also a stranger to the God of Israel.
entries.8f9df9df65969cd2f5e361cf722d189ab54c3785: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen23923" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23924" type="x-p"/> Neither let her take thee with her eye-lids - It is a very general custom in the East to paint the eye-lids. I have many Asiatic drawings in which this is expressed. They have a method of polishing the eyes with a preparation of antimony, so that they appear with an indescribable lustre; or, as one who mentions the fact from observation, "Their eyes appear to be swimming in bliss."
entries.66e787a035bcd16694b65f17c9dda982b11807d0: <hi type="bold">Verse 26</hi> <div eID="gen23924" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23925" type="x-p"/> By means of a whorish woman - In following lewd women, a man is soon reduced to poverty and disease. The Septuagint gives this a strange turn: timh gar pornhv, osh kai enov artou. "For the price or hire of a whore is about one loaf." So many were they in the land, that they hired themselves out for a bare subsistence. The Vulgate, Syriac, and Arabic, give the same sense. The old MS. Bible has it thus: The price forsothe of a strumpet is unneth oon lof: the woman forsothe taketh the precious liif of a mam. The sense of which is, and probably the sense of the Hebrew too, While the man hires the whore for a single loaf of bread; the woman thus hired taketh his precious life. She extracts his energy, and poisons his constitution. In the first clause אשה זונה ishshah zonah is plainly a prostitute; but should we render אשת esheth, in the second clause, an adulteress? I think not. The versions in general join אשת איש esheth ish, together, which, thus connected, signify no more than the wife of a man; and out of this we have made adulteress, and Coverdale a married woman. I do not think that the Old MS. Bible gives a good sense; and it requires a good deal of paraphrase to extract the common meaning from the text. Though the following verses seem to countenance the common interpretation, yet they may contain a complete sense of themselves; but, taken in either way, the sense is good, though the construction is a little violent.
entries.72dd51fe7b783d75e10a319848367a117946b7e7: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen23925" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23926" type="x-p"/> Can a man take fire - These were proverbial expressions, the meaning of which was plain to every capacity.
entries.6ebbe815927c587c2634b5af05b9236a2c011b4f: <hi type="bold">Verse 29</hi> <div eID="gen23926" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23927" type="x-p"/> So he that goeth In to his neighbor's wife - As sure as he who takes fire into his bosom, or who walks upon live coals, is burnt thereby; so sure he that seduces his neighbour's wife shall be guilty. That is, he shall be punished.
entries.b785eb8f90de15b8963b168dc15b0d0440289eb0: <hi type="bold">Verse 30</hi> <div eID="gen23927" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23928" type="x-p"/> Men do not despise a thief if he steal - Every man pities the poor culprit who was perishing for lack of food, and stole to satisfy his hunger; yet no law clears him: he is bound to make restitution; in some cases double, in others quadruple and quintuple; and if he have not property enough to make restitution, to be sold for a bondsman; <reference osisRef="Exo.22.1-Exo.22.4">Exo 22:1-4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.25.39">Lev 25:39</reference>.
entries.202e6b6b6b034443d41b994b10abb0738dc927fc: <hi type="bold">Verse 32</hi> <div eID="gen23928" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23929" type="x-p"/> But whoso committeth adultery - The case understood is that of a married man: he has a wife; and therefore is not in the circumstances of the poor thief, who stole to appease his hunger, having nothing to eat. In this alone the opposition between the two cases is found: the thief had no food, and he stole some; the married man had a wife, and yet went in to the wife of his neighbor. <div eID="gen23929" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23930" type="x-p"/> Destroyeth his own soul - Sins against his life, for, under the law of Moses, adultery was punished with death; <reference osisRef="Lev.20.10">Lev 20:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deu.22.22">Deu 22:22</reference>.
entries.0a1ed8606c076125a2ed838dcee0d120ebb06a2f: <hi type="bold">Verse 33</hi> <div eID="gen23930" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23931" type="x-p"/> A wound and dishonor shall he get - Among the Romans, when a man was caught in the fact, the injured husband took the law into his own hand; and a large radish was thrust up into the anus of the transgressor, which not only overwhelmed him with infamy and disgrace, but generally caused his death.
entries.a67f0e103c038f7fedec571ff16a38c9eb0f22fe: <hi type="bold">Verse 34</hi> <div eID="gen23931" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23932" type="x-p"/> Jealousy is the rage of a man: therefore he will not spare - He will not, when he has detected the adulterer in the fact, wait for the slow progress of the law: it is then to him the day of vengeance; and in general, he avenges himself on the spot, as we see above.
entries.1597c6cd5b6f71e596f520064c1394bd507c0e5e: <hi type="bold">Verse 35</hi> <div eID="gen23932" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23933" type="x-p"/> He will not regard any ransom - This is an injury that admits of no compensation. No gifts can satisfy a man for the injury his honor has sustained; and to take a bribe or a ransom, would be setting up chastity at a price.  <chapter eID="Prov.6"/> <div eID="gen23933" type="x-p"/>

entries.2016371e5abf469851836330911bc474abb0faee: <reference osisRef="Prov.6.1-Prov.6.5">Pro 6:1-5</reference> <div eID="gen10712" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10713" type="x-p"/> The author warns against suretyship; or rather, he advises that if one has made himself surety, he should as quickly as possible withdraw from the snare. 1 My son, if thou hast become surety for thy neighbour,    Hast given thy hand for another: 2 Thou art entangled in the words of thy mouth,    Ensnared in the words of thy mouth. 3 Do this then, my son, and free thyself -    For thou hast come under the power of thy neighbour -    Go, instantly entreat and importune thy neighbour. 4 Give no sleep to thine eyes,    And no slumber to thine eyelids; 5 Tear thyself free like a gazelle from his hand,    And as a bird from the hand of the fowler. <div eID="gen10713" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10714" type="x-p"/> The chief question here is, whether ל after ערב introduces him for whom or with whom one becomes surety. Elsewhere ערב (R. רב, whence also ארב, <hi type="italic">nectere</hi>, to twist close and compact) with the accusative of the person means to become surety for any one, to represent him as a surety, <reference osisRef="Prov.11.15">Pro 11:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.20.16">Pro 20:16</reference> (<reference osisRef="Prov.27.13">Pro 27:13</reference>), <reference osisRef="Gen.43.9">Gen 43:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.44.33">Gen 44:33</reference> (as with the accusative of the matter, to pledge anything, to deposit it as a pledge, <reference osisRef="Jer.30.21">Jer 30:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Neh.5.3">Neh 5:3</reference>, = שׂים, Arab. waḍ'a, <reference osisRef="Job.17.3">Job 17:3</reference>); and to become surety with any one is expressed, <reference osisRef="Gen.17.18">Gen 17:18</reference>, by ערב לפני. The phrase ערב ל is not elsewhere met with, and is thus questionable. If we look to <reference osisRef="Prov.6.3">Pro 6:3</reference>, the רע (רעה) mentioned there cannot possibly be the creditor with whom one has become surety, for so impetuous and urgent an application to him would be both purposeless and unbecoming. But if he is meant for whom one has become surety, then certainly לרעך is also to be understood of the same person, and ל is thus <hi type="italic">dat. commodi</hi>; similar to this is the Targumic ערבוּתא על, suretyship for any one, <reference osisRef="Prov.17.18">Pro 17:18</reference>; Pro 22:26. But is the זר, 1b, distinguished from רעך, the stranger with whom one has become surety? The parallels <reference osisRef="Prov.11.15">Pro 11:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.20.16">Pro 20:16</reference>, where זר denotes the person whom one represents, show that in both lines one and the same person is meant; זר is in the Proverbs equivalent to אחר, each different from the person in the discourse, <reference osisRef="Prov.5.17">Pro 5:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.27.2">Pro 27:2</reference> - thus, like רעך, denotes not the friend, but generally him to whom one stands in any kind of relation, even a very external one, in a word, the fellow-creatures or neighbours, <reference osisRef="Prov.24.28">Pro 24:28</reference> (cf. the Arab. sahbk and ḳarynk, which are used as vaguely and superficially). It is further a question, whether we have to explain 1b: if thou hast given thine hand to another, or for another. Here also we are without evidence from the usage of the language; for the phrase תּקע כּף, or merely תּקע, appears to be used of striking the hand in suretyship where it elsewhere occurs without any further addition, <reference osisRef="Prov.17.18">Pro 17:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.22.26">Pro 22:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.11.15">Pro 11:15</reference>; however, <reference osisRef="Job.17.3">Job 17:3</reference>, נתקע ליד appears the same: to strike into the hand of any one, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, to give to him the hand-stroke. From this passage Hitzig concludes that the surety gave the hand-stroke, without doubt in the presence of witnesses, first of all of the creditor, to the debtor, as a sign that he stood for him. But this idea is unnatural, and the “without doubt” melts into air. He on whose hand the stroke falls is always the person to whom one gives suretyship, and confirms it by the hand-stroke. Job also, <hi type="italic">l.c.</hi>, means to say: who else but Thou, O Lord, could give to me a pledge, viz., of my innocence? If now the זר, v. 1b, is, as we have shown, not the creditor,<note placement="foot">A translation by R. Joseph Joel of Fulda, 1787, whose autograph MS Baer possesses, renders the passage not badly thus: - “My son, if thou hast become surety for thy friend, and hast given the hand to another, then thou art bound by thy word, held by thy promise. Yet do what I say to thee, my son: Be at pains as soon as thou canst to get free, otherwise thou art in the power of thy friend; shun no trouble, be urgent with thy friend.”</note> but the debtor, then is the ל the <hi type="italic">dat. commodi</hi>, as 1a, and the two lines perfectly correspond. תּקע properly means to drive, to strike with a resounding noise, cogn. with the Arab. wak'a, which may be regarded as its intrans. (Fl.); then particularly to strike the hand or with the hand. He to whom this hand-pledge is given for another remains here undesignated. A new question arises, whether in <reference osisRef="Prov.6.6">Pro 6:6</reference>, where נוקשׁ (<hi type="italic">illaqueari</hi>) and נלכּד (<hi type="italic">comprehendi</hi>) follow each other as <reference osisRef="Isa.8.15">Isa 8:15</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.50.24">Jer 50:24</reference>, the hypothetical antecedent is continued or not. We agree with Schultens, Ziegler, and Fleischer against the continuance of the אם. The repetition of the בּאמרי פיך (cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.2.14">Pro 2:14</reference>) serves rightly to strengthen the representation of the thought: thou, thou thyself and no other, hast then ensnared thyself in the net; but this strengthening of the expression would greatly lose in force by placing <reference osisRef="Prov.6.2">Pro 6:2</reference> in the antecedent, while if <reference osisRef="Prov.6.2">Pro 6:2</reference> is regarded as the conclusion, and thus as the principal proposition, it appears in its full strength.
entries.902bef8caa6d88f21f488ebb58f1a148bdffa0d1: <reference osisRef="Prov.6.6-Prov.6.8">Pro 6:6-8</reference> <div eID="gen10717" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10718" type="x-p"/> As Elihu (<reference osisRef="Job.35.11">Job 35:11</reference>) says that God has set the beasts as our teachers, so he sends the sluggard to the school of the ant (<hi type="italic">Ameise</hi>), so named (in Germ.) from its industry (<hi type="italic">Emsigkeit</hi>): 6 Go to the ant, sluggard;    Consider her ways, and be wise! 7 She that hath no judge,    Director, and ruler: 8 She prepareth in summer her food,    Has gathered in harvest her store. <div eID="gen10718" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10719" type="x-p"/> The <hi type="italic">Dechî</hi> written mostly under the לך separates the inseparable. The thought, Go to the ant, sluggard! permits no other distinction than in the vocative; but the <hi type="italic">Dechî</hi> of לך אל־נמלה is changed into <hi type="italic">Munach</hi><note placement="foot">Cod. 1294 accentuates לך אל־נמלה; and that, according to Ben-Asher’s rule, is correct.</note> on account of the nature of the <hi type="italic">Athnach</hi>-word, which consists of only two syllables without the counter-tone. The ant has for its Hebrew-Arabic name נמלה, from the R. נם (Isaiah, p. 687), which is first used of the sound, which expresses the idea of the low, dull, secret - thus of its active and yet unperceived motion; its Aramaic name in the Peshîto, ûmenaa', and in the Targ. שׁוּמשׁמנא (also Arab. sumsum, simsim, of little red ants), designates it after its quick activity, its busy running hither and thither (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Fleischer in Levy’s <hi type="italic">Chald. Wörterb</hi>. ii. 578). She is a model of unwearied and well-planned labour. From the plur. דּרכיה it is to be concluded that the author observed their art in gathering in and laying up in store, carrying burdens, building their houses, and the like (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., the passages in the Talmud and Midrash in the Hamburg <hi type="italic">Real-Encyclopädie für Bibel und Talmud</hi>, 1868, p. 83f.). To the ant the sluggard (עצל, Aram. and Arab. עטל, with the fundamental idea of weight and dulness) is sent, to learn from her to be ashamed, and to be taught wisdom.
entries.9b77fdcf0a927a90b6a0c2a126995da0e148930f: <reference osisRef="Prov.6.9-Prov.6.11">Pro 6:9-11</reference> <div eID="gen10722" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10723" type="x-p"/> After the poet has admonished the sluggard to take the ant as an example, he seeks also to rouse him out of his sleepiness and indolence: 9 How long, O sluggard, wilt thou lie?    When wilt thou rise up from thy sleep? 10 “A little sleep, a little slumber,    A little folding of the hands to rest!” 11 So comes like a strong robber thy poverty,    And thy want as an armed man.  <reference osisRef="Prov.6.9-Prov.6.10">Pro 6:9-10</reference> <div eID="gen10723" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10724" type="x-p"/> The awakening cry, <reference osisRef="Prov.6.9">Pro 6:9</reference>, is not of the kind that Paul could have it in his mind, Eph 5:14. עצל has, as the vocative, <hi type="italic">Pasek</hi> after it, and is, on account of the <hi type="italic">Pasek</hi>, in correct editions accentuated not with <hi type="italic">Munach</hi>, but <hi type="italic">Mercha</hi>. The words, <reference osisRef="Prov.6.10">Pro 6:10</reference>, are not an ironical call (sleep only yet a little while, but in truth a long while), but <hi type="italic">per mimesin</hi> the reply of the sluggard with which he turns away the unwelcome disturber. The plurals with מעט sound like self-delusion: yet a little, but a sufficient! To fold the hands, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, to cross them over the breast, or put them into the bosom, denotes also, <reference osisRef="Eccl.4.5">Ecc 4:5</reference>, the idler. חבּוּק, <hi type="italic">complicatio</hi> (cf. in Livy, <hi type="italic">compressis quod aiunt manibus sidere</hi>; and Lucan, 2:292, <hi type="italic">compressas tenuisse manus</hi>), for formed like שׁקּוּי, <reference osisRef="Prov.3.8">Pro 3:8</reference>, and the <hi type="italic">inf</hi>. שׁכב like חסר, <reference osisRef="Prov.10.21">Pro 10:21</reference>, and שׁפל, Pro 16:19. The <hi type="italic">perf. consec</hi>. connects itself with the words heard from the mouth of the sluggard, which are as a hypothetical antecedent thereto: if thou so sayest, and always again sayest, then this is the consequence, that suddenly and inevitably poverty and want come upon thee. That מהלּך denotes the <hi type="italic">grassator</hi>, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, vagabond (Arab. dawwar, one who wanders much about), or the robber or foe (like the Arab. 'aduww, properly <hi type="italic">transgressor finium</hi>), is not justified by the usage of the language; הלך signifies, <reference osisRef="2Sam.12.4">2Sa 12:4</reference>, the traveller, and מהלּך is one who rides quickly forward, not directly a κακὸς ὁδοιπόρος (lxx).
entries.d694eabdfeb5ae90ed16bdacc71b3ebb45fdc687: <reference osisRef="Prov.6.12-Prov.6.15">Pro 6:12-15</reference> <div eID="gen10725" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10726" type="x-p"/> There follows now a third brief series of instructions, which run to a conclusion with a deterring prospect similar to the foregoing. 12 A worthless man, a wicked man,      Is he who practiseth falsehood with his mouth; 13 Who winketh with his eyes, scrapeth with his foot,      Pointeth with his fingers. 14 Malice is in his heart,      He deviseth evil at all times,      He spreadeth strife. 15 Therefore suddenly his destruction shall come,      Suddenly shall he be destroyed, and there is no remedy. <div eID="gen10726" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10727" type="x-p"/> It is a question, what is the subject and what the predicate in Pro 6:12. Thus much is clear, that upon him who is here described according to his deceitful conduct the sentence of condemnation shall fall. He who is so described is thus subject, and אדם בּליּעל is without doubt predicate. But does the complex subject begin with אישׁ און? Thus <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, Hitzig: “A worthless man is the wicked man who....” But the interchange of עדם and אישׁ is a sign of parallel relation; and if 12b belonged attributively to אישׁ און, then since אישׁ האון is not used, it ought at least to have been continued by ההולך. The general moral categories, 12a, are thus predicates, as was indeed besides probable; the copious division of the subject demands also in point of style a more developed predicate. <reference osisRef="Prov.16.27">Pro 16:27</reference> is simpler in plan, and also logically different. There the expression is, as is usual, אישׁ בליעל. Since אדם און is not possible, the author uses instead בליעל. This word, composed of בּלי and יעל (from יעל, ועל, to be useful, to be good for), so fully serves as one word, that it even takes the article, 1Sa 25:25. It denotes worthlessness, generally in a chain of words in the genitive, but also the worthless, <reference osisRef="Job.34.18">Job 34:18</reference>; and it is to be so taken here, for אדם does not form a <hi type="italic">constructivus</hi>, and never governs a genitive. בליעל is thus a virtual adjective (as <hi type="italic">nequam</hi> in <hi type="italic">homo nequam</hi>); the connection is like that of אדם רשׁע, <reference osisRef="Prov.11.7">Pro 11:7</reference>, and elsewhere, although more appositional than this pure attributive. Synonymous with בליעל is און (from <hi type="italic">an</hi>, to breathe), wickedness, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, want of all moral character. Thus worthless and wicked is he who practises deceit with his mouth (cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.4.24">Pro 4:24</reference>), <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, who makes language the means of untruthfulness and uncharitableness. עקּשׁוּת פּה is meant in a moral sense, but without excluding that distortion of the mouth which belongs to the mimicry of the malicious. It is the accus. of the object; for הלך is also bound in a moral sense with the accusative of that which one practises, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, dealing with, exercises himself in, <reference osisRef="Prov.2.7">Pro 2:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.28.18">Pro 28:18</reference>, Isa 33:15.
entries.c04f00fc1bad0bc18c4cbcb6e00d754c00358a4c: <reference osisRef="Prov.6.16-Prov.6.19">Pro 6:16-19</reference> <div eID="gen10730" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10731" type="x-p"/> What now follows is not a separate section (Hitzig), but the corroborative continuation of that which precedes. The last word (מדנים, strife) before the threatening of punishment, 14b, is also here the last. The thought that no vice is a greater abomination to God than the (in fact satanical) striving to set men at variance who love one another, clothes itself in the form of the numerical proverb which we have already considered, pp. 12, 13. From that place we transfer the translation of this example of a <hi type="italic">Midda</hi>: - 16 There are six things which Jahve hateth,      And seven are an abhorrence to His soul: 17 Haughty eyes, a lying tongue,      And hands that shed innocent blood; 18 An heart that deviseth the thoughts of evil,      Feet that hastily run to wickedness, 19 One that uttereth lies as a false witness,      And he who soweth strife between brethren. <div eID="gen10731" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10732" type="x-p"/> The sense is not, that the six things are hateful to God, and the seventh an abomination to Him besides (Löwenstein); the <hi type="italic">Midda</hi>-form in <reference osisRef="Amos.1.3-Amos.2.6">Amos 1:3-2:6</reference>, and in the proverb in <reference osisRef="Job.5.19">Job 5:19</reference>, shows that the seven are to be numbered separately, and the seventh is the <hi type="italic">non plus ultra</hi> of all that is hated by God. We are not to translate: <hi type="italic">sex haecce odit</hi>, for המּה, הנּה, (הם, הן) points backwards and hitherwards, but not, as אלּה, forwards to that immediately following; in that case the words would be שׁשׁ אלה, or more correctly האלה שׁשׁ. But also Hitzig’s explanation, “These six things (viz., <reference osisRef="Prov.6.12-Prov.6.15">Pro 6:12-15</reference>) Jahve hateth,” is impossible; for (which is also against that <hi type="italic">haecce</hi>) the substantive pronoun המה nuonorp , הנה (ההמה, ההנה) is never, like the Chald. המּון (המּו), employed as an accus. in the sense of אתהם, אתהן, it is always (except where it is the virtual gen. connected with a preposition) only the nom., whether of the subject or of the predicate; and where it is the nom. of the predicate, as <reference osisRef="Deut.20.15">Deu 20:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.51.19">Isa 51:19</reference>, substantival clauses precede in which הנה (המה) represents the substantive verb, or, more correctly, in which the logical copula resulting from the connection of the clause itself remains unexpressed. Accordingly, 'שׂנא ה is a relative clause, and is therefore so accentuated here, as at <reference osisRef="Prov.30.15">Pro 30:15</reference> and elsewhere: <hi type="italic">sex</hi> (<hi type="italic">sunt</hi>) <hi type="italic">ea quae Deus odit, et septem</hi> (<hi type="italic">sunt</hi>) <hi type="italic">abominatio animae ejus</hi>. Regarding the statement that the soul of God hates anything, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., at Isa 1:14. תועבות, an error in the writing occasioned by the numeral (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., <reference osisRef="Prov.26.25">Pro 26:25</reference>), is properly corrected by the Kerı̂; the poet had certainly the singular in view, as <reference osisRef="Prov.3.32">Pro 3:32</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.11.1">Pro 11:1</reference>, when he wrote תועבת. The first three characteristics are related to each other as mental, verbal, actual, denoted by the members of the body by means of which these characteristics come to light. The virtues are taken all together as a body (organism), and meekness is its head. Therefore there stands above all, as the sin of sins, the <hi type="italic">mentis elatae tumor</hi>, which expresses itself in <hi type="italic">elatum</hi> (<hi type="italic">grande</hi>) <hi type="italic">supercilium</hi>: עינים רמות, the feature of the רם, haughty (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.18.28">Psa 18:28</reference> with <reference osisRef="2Sam.22.28">2Sa 22:28</reference>), is the opposite of the feature of the שׁח עינים, <reference osisRef="Job.22.29">Job 22:29</reference>; עין is in the O.T. almost always (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Sol 4:9) fem., and adjectives of course form no dual. The second of these characteristics is the lying tongue, and the third the murderous hands. דּם־נקי is innocent blood as distinguished from דּם הנּקי, the blood of the innocent, Deu 19:13.<note placement="foot">The writing דּם follows the Masoretic rule, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Kimchi, <hi type="italic">Michlol</hi> 205b, and Heidenheim under <reference osisRef="Deut.19.10">Deu 19:10</reference>, where in printed editions of the text (also in Norzi’s) the irregular form דּם נקי is found. Besides, the <hi type="italic">Metheg</hi> is to be given to דּם־, so that one may not read it dom, as <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, שׁשׁ־מאות, <reference osisRef="Gen.7.11">Gen 7:11</reference>, that one may not read it שׁשׁ־.</note>
entries.7fc361e457eb4f36a2bf03a2b1c338b2c6dee8ec: <reference osisRef="Prov.6.20-Prov.6.21">Pro 6:20-21</reference> <div eID="gen10735" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10736" type="x-p"/> After these three smaller sections, the teacher of wisdom returns here to the theme of the eighth: Warning against sins of the flesh, whose power and prevalence among men is so immeasurably great, that their terrible consequences cannot sufficiently be held up before them, particularly before youth. 20 Keep, my son, the commandment of thy father,      And reject not the instruction of thy mother. 21 Bind them to thy heart evermore,      Fasten them about thy neck. <div eID="gen10736" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10737" type="x-p"/> The suff. -ēm refers to the good doctrine (cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.7.3">Pro 7:3</reference>) pointed out by מצוה and תּורה; the masc. stands, as is usual (<hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, <reference osisRef="Prov.1.16">Pro 1:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.5.2">Pro 5:2</reference>), instead of the fem. Regarding the figure, reminding us of the Tefillin and of Amuletes for perpetual representation, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., under Pro 3:3. Similarly of persons, Sol 8:6. The verb ענד (only here and <reference osisRef="Job.31.36">Job 31:36</reference>) signifies to bend, particularly to bend aside (Arab. 'ind, bending off, going aside; accus. as adv., aside, <hi type="italic">apud</hi>), and to bend up, to wind about, <hi type="italic">circumplicare</hi>.
entries.8eebbcad651dbba17454a0faad1a3d53570c3dd6: <reference osisRef="Prov.6.22">Pro 6:22</reference> <div eID="gen10737" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10738" type="x-p"/> The representation of the good doctrine is now personified, and becomes identified with it. <div eID="gen10738" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10739" type="x-p"/> When thou walkest, it will guide thee; <div eID="gen10739" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10740" type="x-p"/> When thou liest down, it will keep watch over thee; <div eID="gen10740" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10741" type="x-p"/> And when thou wakest, it will talk with thee. <div eID="gen10741" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10742" type="x-p"/> The subject is the doctrine of wisdom, with which the representation of wisdom herself is identified. The futures are not expressive of a wish or of an admonition, but of a promise; the form of the third clause shows this. Thus, and in the same succession as in the <hi type="italic">schema</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.6.7">Deu 6:7</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.11.19">Pro 11:19</reference>, are the three circumstances of the outward life distinguished: going, lying down, and rising up. The punctuation בּהתהלכך, found here and there, is Ben-Naphtali’s variant; Ben-Asher and also the <hi type="italic">Textus rec</hi>. reject the <hi type="italic">Metheg</hi> in this case, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Baer’s <hi type="italic">Metheg</hi>-<hi type="italic">Setzung</hi>, §28. The verb נחה, with its <hi type="italic">Hiph</hi>. in a strengthened <hi type="italic">Kal</hi>-signification, is more frequently found in the Psalms than in the Proverbs; the Arab. nh' shows that it properly signifies to direct (<hi type="italic">dirigere</hi>), to give direction, to move in a definite direction. שׁמר with על, to take into protection, we had already <reference osisRef="Prov.2.11">Pro 2:11</reference>; this author has favourite forms of expression, in the repetition of which he takes delight. With lying down, sleeping is associated. והקיצות is, as <reference osisRef="Ps.139.18">Psa 139:18</reference>, the <hi type="italic">hypoth. perf</hi>., according to Ewald, §357a: <hi type="italic">et ut expergefactus es, illa te compellabit</hi>. Bertheau incorrectly: she will make thee thoughtful. But apart from the fact that there is no evidence of the existence of this <hi type="italic">Hiph</hi>. in the language of the Bible, the personification demands a clearer figure. שׂיח (שׂוּח) signifies mental speech and audible speech (<reference osisRef="Gen.24.63">Gen 24:63</reference>, poet., in the Talmudic<note placement="foot">The conjecture thrown out by Wetstein, that (Arab.) shykh is equivalent to משׂיח (מסיח), speaker, is untenable, since the verb shakh, to be old, a so-called munsarif, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, conjugated throughout, is used in all forms, and thus is certainly the root of the shykh.</note> a common word); with ב, speaking concerning something (<hi type="italic">fabulari de</hi>), <reference osisRef="Ps.69.13">Psa 69:13</reference>; with the accus., that which is said of a thing, <reference osisRef="Ps.145.5">Psa 145:5</reference>, or the address, briefly for שׂיח ל, <reference osisRef="Job.12.8">Job 12:8</reference> (as מגּן with accus. <reference osisRef="Prov.4.9">Pro 4:9</reference> = מגן ל): when thou art awake, wisdom will forthwith enter into conversation with thee, and fill thy thoughts with right matter, and give to thy hands the right direction and consecration.
entries.fc37aef9d22240b45f293a5d5814033cc0069909: <reference osisRef="Prov.6.23">Pro 6:23</reference> <div eID="gen10742" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10743" type="x-p"/> Since in היא the idea of wisdom and of wholesome doctrine lie in one another, the author can proceed with proof: <div eID="gen10743" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10744" type="x-p"/> For a lamp is the commandment, and instruction a light (Jerome <hi type="italic">et lex lux</hi>); <div eID="gen10744" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10745" type="x-p"/> And a way of life, disciplinary reproofs. <div eID="gen10745" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10746" type="x-p"/> That תורה has here not the positive, specifically Israelitish sense, but the generalized sense of instruction in conformity with truth regarding the will of God and the duty of man, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., p. 42. This instruction mediated by man, but of divine origin, is אור, light, which enlightens the man who submits to it; and the commandment, מצוה, which directs men in every case to do what is right, and forbids that which is wrong (including the prohibition <reference osisRef="Lev.4.2">Lev 4:2</reference>), is נר, a lamp which, kindled at that light, enlightens all the darkness of ignorance with reference to human conduct and its consequences. אור and נר are related to each other as general and particular, primary and derivative. Löwenstein accentuates incorrectly תּורהו אור instead of תּורהו אור (as the Cod. 1294 and the 3 Erfurt Codd.); <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., on the retrogression of the tone, not existing here, under Pro 3:15. The gen. מוּסר denotes the object or character of the admonition: not disciplinary in the external sense of the word, but rather moral, having in view discipline in the sense of education, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, moral edification and elevation. Such corrections are דּרך חיּים, the way to true life, direction how to obtain it.
entries.cc567dbfa1cfe48632e5d4f798f5b452de2c4b50: <reference osisRef="Prov.6.24">Pro 6:24</reference> <div eID="gen10746" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10747" type="x-p"/> The section thus closes: <div eID="gen10747" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10748" type="x-p"/> To keep thee from the vile woman, <div eID="gen10748" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10749" type="x-p"/> From the flattery of the strange tongue. <div eID="gen10749" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10750" type="x-p"/> Regarding the genitive connection אושׁת רע, a woman of a wicked character, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., under <reference osisRef="Prov.2.14">Pro 2:14</reference>; and regarding the adjectival connection לשׁון נכריה, under <reference osisRef="Prov.6.17">Pro 6:17</reference>; the strange tongue is the tongue (לשׁון) of the strange (foreign) woman (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., p. 81), alluring with smooth words (<reference osisRef="Prov.2.16">Pro 2:16</reference>). Ewald, Bertheau: from her of a smooth tongue, the stranger, as Symm., Theod., ἀπὸ λειογλώσσου ξένης; but חלקת is a substantive (<reference osisRef="Gen.27.16">Gen 27:16</reference>), and as a fem. adject. form is without an example. Rather חלקת לשׁון is to be regarded as the first member and נכריה as the second of the st. constr., for the former constitutes one idea, and לשון on this account remains unabbreviated; cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.68.22">Psa 68:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.28.1">Isa 28:1</reference>; but (1) this syntactical phenomenon is yet problematical, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Friedr. Philippi, <hi type="italic">Wesen und Ursprung des St. Constr</hi>. p. 17; and (2) the supposition of such an anomaly is here unnecessary.
entries.a71a41a2e9c971e3ee65687160decf64b1600ed3: <reference osisRef="Prov.6.25-Prov.6.26">Pro 6:25-26</reference> <div eID="gen10750" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10751" type="x-p"/> The <hi type="italic">proaemium</hi> of these twelve proverbial discourses is now at an end. Wisdom herself begins striking the note of the Decalogue: 25 Long not for her beauty in thy heart,      And let her not catch thee with her eyelids; 26 Because for a harlot one cometh down to a piece of bread,      And a man’s wife lieth in wait for a precious soul. <div eID="gen10751" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10752" type="x-p"/> The warning 25a is in the spirit of the “thou shalt not covet,” <reference osisRef="Exod.20.17">Exo 20:17</reference>, and the ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ αὑτοῦ, <reference osisRef="Matt.5.28">Mat 5:28</reference>, of the Preacher on the Mount. The Talmudic proverb הרהודי עבירה קשו מעבירה (<hi type="italic">Joma</hi> 29a) means only that the imagination of the sinful act exhausts the body even more than the act itself. The warning, “let her not catch thee with her eyelids,” refers to her (the adulteress’s) coquettish ogling and amorous winking. In the reason added, beginning with כּי בעד־ (thus it is to be punctuated), there is the appositional connection אשּׁה זונה, Gesen. §113; the idea of זונה goes over into 26b. “לחם כּכּר [ = כּרכּר, R. kr, to round, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., at Gen 49:5], properly a circle of bread, is a small round piece of bread, such as is still baked in Italy (<hi type="italic">pagnotta</hi>) and in the East (Arab. ḳurṣ), here an expression for the smallest piece” (Fl.). בּעד (<hi type="italic">constr</hi>. of בּעד), as <reference osisRef="Job.2.4">Job 2:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.32.14">Isa 32:14</reference>, is used in the sense of ὑπέρ, <hi type="italic">pro</hi>, and with עד there is connected the idea of the coming down to this low point. Ewald, Bertheau explain after the lxx, τιμὴ γὰρ πόρνης ὅση καὶ ἑνὸς ἄρτου, γυνὴ δὲ ἀνδρῶν τιμίας ψυχὰς ἀγρεύει. But nothing is said here of price (reward); the parallelism is synonymous, not antithetic: he is doubly threatened with loss who enters upon such a course. The adulterer squanders his means (<reference osisRef="Prov.29.3">Pro 29:3</reference>) to impoverishment (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., the mention of a loaf of bread in the description of poverty <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.36">1Sa 2:36</reference>), and a man’s wife (but at the same time seeking converse with another) makes a prey of a precious soul; for whoever consents to adulterous converse with her, loses not perhaps his means, but certainly freedom, purity, dignity of soul, yea, his own person. צוּד comprehends - as צידון, fisher’s town [Zidon], Arab. ṣyâd, hunter and fisher, show - all kinds of hunting, but in Hebr. is used only of the hunting of wild beasts. The root-meaning (cf. צדיּה) is to spy, to seize.
entries.959fd083ca635a1517ff7ba37bd4850f1adb427c: <reference osisRef="Prov.6.27-Prov.6.29">Pro 6:27-29</reference> <div eID="gen10752" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10753" type="x-p"/> The moral necessity of ruinous consequences which the sin of adultery draws after it, is illustrated by examples of natural cause and effect necessarily connected: 27 Can one take fire in his bosom      And his clothes not be burned? 28 Or can any one walk over burning coals      And his feet not be burned? 29 So he that goeth to his neighbour’s wife,      No one remains unpunished that toucheth her. <div eID="gen10753" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10754" type="x-p"/> We would say: Can any one, without being, etc.; the former is the Semitic “extended (paratactic)<note placement="foot">The παρατακτικὸς χρόνος denotes the imperfect tense, because it is still extended to the future.</note> construction.” The first אישׁ has the conjunctive <hi type="italic">Shalsheleth</hi>. חתה signifies to seize and draw forth a brand or coal with the fire-tongs or shovel (מחתּה, the instrument for this); cf. Arab. khât, according to Lane, “he seized or snatched away a thing;” the form יחתּה is <hi type="italic">Kal</hi>, as יחנה (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Köhler, <hi type="italic">De Tetragammate</hi>, 1867, p. 10). חיק (properly indentation) is here not the lap, but, as <reference osisRef="Isa.40.11">Isa 40:11</reference>, the bosom.
entries.0f5ed50e0c777cd99584c398f19621c00068df5d: <reference osisRef="Prov.6.30-Prov.6.31">Pro 6:30-31</reference> <div eID="gen10756" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10757" type="x-p"/> The thief and the adulterer are now placed in comparison with one another, in such a way that adultery is supposed to be a yet greater crime. 30 One does not treat the thief scornfully if he steals      To satisfy his craving when he is hungry; 31 Being seized, he may restore sevenfold,      Give up the whole wealth of his house. <div eID="gen10757" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10758" type="x-p"/> For the most part 30a is explained: even when this is the case, one does not pass it over in the thief as a bagatelle. Ewald remarks: בּוּז ל stands here in its nearest signification of overlooking, whence first follows that of contemning. But this “nearest” signification is devised wholly in favour of this passage; - the interpretation, “they do not thus let the thief pass,” is set aside by Sol 8:1, Sol 8:7; for by 31b, cf. Sol 8:7, and 34a, cf. Sol 8:6, it is proved that from <reference osisRef="Prov.6.30">Pro 6:30</reference> on, reminiscences from the Canticles, which belong to the literature of the <hi type="italic">Chokma</hi>, find their way into the Mashal language of the author. Hitzig’s correct supposition, that בּוּז ל always signifies positive contemning, does not necessitate the interrogative interpretation: “Does not one despise the thief if...?” Thus to be understood, the author ought to have written אף כי or גם כי. Michaelis rightly: <hi type="italic">furtum licet merito pro infami in republica habetur, tamen si cum adulterio comparatur, minus probrosum est</hi>. Regarding נפשׁ in the sense of appetite, and even throat and stomach, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., <hi type="italic">Psychologie</hi>, p. 204. A second is, that the thief, if he is seized (but we regard ונמצא not as the <hi type="italic">hypoth. perf</hi>., but as the <hi type="italic">part. deprehensus</hi>), may make compensation for this crime. The fut. ישׁלּם thus to be understood as the potential lies near from this, that a sevenfold compensation of the thing stolen is unheard of in the Israelitish law; it knows only of a twofold, fourfold, fivefold restoration, Ex. 21:37; <reference osisRef="Exod.22.1-Exod.22.3">Exo 22:1-3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.22.8">Exo 22:8</reference> (cf. Saalschütz, <hi type="italic">Mos. Recht</hi>, p. 554ff.). This excess over that which the law rendered necessary leads into the region of free-will: he (the thief, by which we are now only to think of him whom bitter necessity has made such) may make compensation sevenfold, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, superabundantly; he may give up the whole possessions (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., on הון at <reference osisRef="Prov.1.13">Pro 1:13</reference>) of his house, so as not merely to satisfy the law, but to appease him against whom he has done wrong, and again to gain for himself an honoured name. What is said in <reference osisRef="Prov.6.30">Pro 6:30</reference> and <reference osisRef="Prov.6.31">Pro 6:31</reference> is perfectly just. One does not contemn a man who is a thief through poverty, he is pitied; while the adulterer goes to ruin under all circumstances of contempt and scorn. And: theft may be made good, and that abundantly; but adultery and its consequences are irreparable.
entries.c0fca4ea5d20d4fcde14699f25f7c58fdf3a78bd: <reference osisRef="Prov.6.32-Prov.6.33">Pro 6:32-33</reference> <div eID="gen10758" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10759" type="x-p"/> Here there is a contrast stated to <reference osisRef="Prov.6.30">Pro 6:30</reference> : <reference osisRef="Prov.6.32">32</reference> He who commits adultery (<hi type="italic">adulterans mulierem</hi>) is beside himself,      A self-destroyer-who does this. 33 He gains stripes and disgrace,      And his reproach is never quenched. נאף, which primarily seems to mean <hi type="italic">excedere</hi>, to indulge in excess, is, as also in the Decalogue, cf. <reference osisRef="Lev.20.10">Lev 20:10</reference>, transitive: ὁ μοιχεύων γυναῖκα. Regarding being mad (<hi type="italic">herzlos</hi> = <hi type="italic">heartless</hi>) = <hi type="italic">amens</hi> (<hi type="italic">excors, vecors</hi>), <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., <hi type="italic">Psychologie</hi>, p. 254. משׁחית נפשׁו is he who goes to ruin with wilful perversity. A self-murderer - <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, he intends to ruin his position and his prosperity in life - who does it, viz., this, that he touches the wife of another. It is the worst and most inextinguishable dishonouring of oneself. Singularly Behaji: who annihilates it (his soul), with reference to Deu 21:12. Eccl. 4:17, where עשׂה would be equivalent to בּטּל, καταργεῖν, which is untrue and impossible.<note placement="foot">Behaji ought rather to have referred to Zep 3:19; <reference osisRef="Ezek.7.27">Eze 7:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.22.14">Eze 22:14</reference>; but there עשׂה את means <hi type="italic">agere cum aliquo</hi>, as we say: <hi type="italic">mit jemandem abrechnen</hi> (to settle accounts with any one).</note> נגע refers to the corporal punishment inflicted on the adulterer by the husband (<reference osisRef="Deut.17.8">Deu 17:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.21.5">Deu 21:5</reference>); Hitzig, who rejects <reference osisRef="Prov.6.32">Pro 6:32</reference>, refers it to the stripes which were given to the thief according to the law, but these would be called מכּה (מכּות). The punctuation נגע־וקלון is to be exchanged for קלונו נגע (Löwenstein and other good editors). מצא has a more active signification than our “<hi type="italic">finden</hi>” (to find): <hi type="italic">consequitur</hi>, τυγχάνει.
entries.fe65392802b55a1dd273aa8e0220fe4a92c81a6c: <reference osisRef="Prov.6.34-Prov.6.35">Pro 6:34-35</reference> <div eID="gen10759" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10760" type="x-p"/> One who has been stolen from is to be appeased, but not the injured husband. 34 For jealousy is the fury of a husband,      And he spareth not in the day of vengeance. 35 He regardeth not any ransom,      And is not contented though thou offerest to him gifts ever so great. <div eID="gen10760" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10761" type="x-p"/> The connection marks קנאה as the subject; for it respects carnal intercourse with another’s wife. Jealousy is not usually חמה, the glow of anger (from יחם, as שׁנה from ישׁן), but חמת־גּבר (constr. as שׂנת), the glow of a man’s anger, who with the putting forth of all his manly strength will seek satisfaction to his wounded honour. גּבר, here significant for אישׁ, with the fundamental idea of strength, firmness; cf. Arab. jabr, to make fast, to put right again something broken in pieces, particularly a broken vessel, hence <hi type="italic">Algebra</hi>, properly the operation by which an incomplete magnitude is completed (Fl.). The following ולא־יחמּל (with the orthophonic <hi type="italic">Dagesh</hi>, as <reference osisRef="Prov.6.25">Pro 6:25</reference> יחמּד, and with <hi type="italic">Makkeph</hi>) is connected with גבר, with definite reference to the man whom the faithless guest has made a cuckold. When the day comes in which the adultery brought to light demands and admits of vengeance, then, wounded in his right and in his honour, he knows no mercy; he pays no regard to any atonement or recompense by which the adulterer seeks to appease him and induce him not to inflict the punishment that is due: he does not consent, even though thou makest ever so great the gift whereby thou thinkest to gain him. The phrase נשׂא פנים, πρόσωπον λαμβάνειν, signifies elsewhere to receive the countenance, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, the appearance and the impression of a man, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, to let it impress one favourably; here it is used of the כּפר, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, the means by which covering, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, non-punishment, pardon of the crime, impunity of the guilty, is obtained. Regarding אבה, to consent to, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., at Pro 1:10. שׂחד, Aram. שׂוּחד, is a gift, particularly bribery. That the language may again finally assume the form of an address, it beautifully rounds itself off.  <chapter eID="Prov.6"/> <div eID="gen10761" type="x-p"/>

                  <ns0:head>CHAP. VI.</ns0:head>
                  <ns0:p n="1">1. MY son, if thou be <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ch. 22. 26.</ns0:note> surety <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">To wit, rashly, without considering for whom, or how far thou dost oblige thy self, or how thou shalt discharge the Debt, if occasion require it. Otherwise suretyship in some cases may be not only lawful, but an Act of Justice, and Prudence, and Chari<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ty. See <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 42. 37. & 43. 8. <ns0:hi>Philem. v.</ns0:hi> 19. Or, <ns0:hi>to</ns0:hi> (as this pre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fix most commonly signifies) <ns0:hi>a friend.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> for thy friend, if thou hast stricken thy hand <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Obliged thy self by gi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ving thine Hand, or joining thine Hands with another mans, as the custom then was in such cases: Of which see <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi> 17. 3. <ns0:hi>Prov.</ns0:hi> 17. 8. and 22. 26.</ns0:note> with a stranger <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">With the Creditor, whom he calls a <ns0:hi>Stranger,</ns0:hi> be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cause the Usurers in <ns0:hi>Israel,</ns0:hi> who lent Money to others for their ne<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cessary occasions, upon condition of paying use for it, were either Heathens, or were reputed as bad as Heathens, because this pra<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ctice was forbidden by Gods Law, <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 23. 19. Or, <ns0:hi>to</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>for</ns0:hi> 1 <ns0:hi>Stranger;</ns0:hi> for here is the same prefix which is rendred <ns0:hi>for</ns0:hi> in the for<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mer clause. And so he may imply, that whether a man be surety to, or for, a friend, or to, or for, a stranger, the case and course to be used is much of the same kind.</ns0:note>:</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="2">2. Thou art snared <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">Thy Freedom is lost, and thou art now in Bondage to ano<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther.</ns0:note> with the words of thy mouth, thou art taken with the words of thy mouth.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="3">3. Do this now, my son, and deliver thy self, when thou art come into the hand <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Into the Power.</ns0:note> of thy friend <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Either 1. Of the Creditor, who possibly may be also thy Friend; yet take the following course with him, and much more if he be a Stranger. Or 2. Of the Debtor, for whom, as being thy Friend, thou didst become Sure<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ty; whereby thou art not only in the Creditors Power<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> to exact payment, but also in the Debtors Power, by his neglect or unfaith<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fulness, to expose thee to the payment of the Debt. And this may seem best to agree both with <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 1. where <ns0:hi>Friend</ns0:hi> is taken in that sense, and is distinguished from the Creditor who is called a <ns0:hi>stranger,</ns0:hi> and with the words here following; for this <ns0:hi>humbling of himself</ns0:hi> was not likely to have much power with a Stranger, and a griping U<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />surer; but it might probably prevail with his Friend, either to take effectual care to pay the Debt, or at least to discharge him from the obligation, or to secure him against it some other way.</ns0:note>, go, hum<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ble thy self <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Heb. <ns0:hi>Offer thy self to be trodden upon,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Throw thy self down</ns0:hi> at his feet. As thou hast made thy self his Servant, bear the fruits of thine own Folly, and humbly and earnestly implore his Patience and Cle<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mency.</ns0:note>, <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> so shalt thou prevail with thy friend<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g>
                     </ns0:note> and make sure thy friend.<ns0:note place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>h</ns0:hi> Or, <ns0:hi>and prevail with thy Friend,</ns0:hi> strive to win him by thine incessant and earnest solicitations. Or, <ns0:hi>honour</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>magnifie thy Friend,</ns0:hi> which is fitly and properly opposed to, and indeed is in some good measure done by the humbling a mans self before him.</ns0:note>
                  </ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="4">4. Give not sleep to thine eyes, nor slumber to thine eye-lids <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">To wit, until thou hast taken care for the discharge of this obligation. Be not secure, nor negligent, nor dilatory in this mat<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ter.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="5">5. Deliver thy self as a roe from the hand <ns0:hi>of the Hunter</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">With all possible expedition, as the Roe runs swiftly away.</ns0:note>, and as a bird from the hand of the fowler.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="6">6. Go to the ant <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">This is another distinct precept; and it is for the most part as needless to seek, as hard to find, Coherence in the Proverbs and Counsels of this Book.</ns0:note>, thou sluggard, consider her ways <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Her actions and manner of living, espe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cially her Diligence and Providence, which are the things com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mended in her, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 7, 8. of which Naturalists give many Instances, as that the Ants watch the fittest seasons for all things, that they provide most plentifully against the time of Famine, that they ne<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ver hinder, but always assist one another in their work, and unite their force together to carry away such things as are too large or heavy for one of them, that they prepare fit cells or repositories for their Corn in the ground, and such as the Rain cannot easily reach; and if through excessive rain their Corn be wet, they bring it forth to be dried, that they bite off the ends of the Grains of Corn that they may not grow, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note>, and be wise:</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="7">
                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:521" />7. Which having no guide, overseer, or ruler <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Which might direct them in, or quicken them to the work, as the Bees have their Kings, and many other Creatures have their Leaders. This heightens their commendation.</ns0:note>,</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="8">8. Provideth her meat in the summer, <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> gathereth her food in the harvest <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">When they come forth in great numbers, as in Winter they stir not out of their holes.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>

                  <ns0:p n="20">20. <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 1. 8.</ns0:note> My son, keep thy fathers commandment <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">So far as it is not contrary to Gods command.</ns0:note>, and forsake not the law of thy mother <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Whom Children are too apt to despise.                   <ns0:p n="31">31. But <ns0:hi>if</ns0:hi> he be found, he shall restore seven-fold <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">
